overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Heidegger's analysis of equipment. You'll be asked about equipment and the in-order-to, readiness-to-hand, the three modes of breakdown, and presence-at-hand as a derivative mode.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Heidegger say that, strictly speaking, there is no such thing as "an" equipment?

options.html: Because every tool is ultimately made of the same basic matter
options.text: Because every tool is ultimately made of the same basic matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger's point isn't about matter. An item of equipment is what it is only within a whole of other equipment, through its in-order-to.

options.html: Because each item is what it is only within a whole of equipment
options.text: Because each item is what it is only within a whole of equipment
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Equipment points beyond itself in-order-to something, so each item belongs to a whole of other equipment, which comes first.

options.html: Because equipment exists only in the mind of the one who uses it
options.text: Because equipment exists only in the mind of the one who uses it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger doesn't locate equipment in the mind. Each item belongs to a whole of other equipment in the world.

options.html: Because tools become objects only when scientists measure them
options.text: Because tools become objects only when scientists measure them
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That concerns presence-at-hand. The point here is that each item of equipment belongs to a whole of other equipment.

forms.stemHtml: A pianist plays a fast passage, attending to the phrasing while the keys go unnoticed. How does Heidegger describe the keys in this moment?

options.html: As present-at-hand, since they're physical objects with properties
options.text: As present-at-hand, since they're physical objects with properties
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. In skilled use, the keys aren't regarded as objects with properties. They're ready-to-hand, withdrawn while the pianist attends to the music.

options.html: As unconscious, since the pianist has no awareness at all
options.text: As unconscious, since the pianist has no awareness at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Use has its own sight, circumspection. The pianist is aware of the phrasing. The keys are ready-to-hand, withdrawn from focal attention.

options.html: As ready-to-hand, withdrawn while circumspection guides the task
options.text: As ready-to-hand, withdrawn while circumspection guides the task
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! In use, equipment withdraws, and circumspection attends to the task: here, the phrasing.

options.html: As obstinate, since they stand between the pianist and the music
options.text: As obstinate, since they stand between the pianist and the music
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Obstinacy is a mode of breakdown, when something gets in the way. Here nothing has gone wrong. The keys are ready-to-hand.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are true of presence-at-hand, on Heidegger's account? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: A thing shows up as a bare object with properties
options.text: A thing shows up as a bare object with properties
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Present-at-hand things are regarded as bare objects with properties, detached from use.

options.html: It comes into view when equipment breaks down
options.text: It comes into view when equipment breaks down
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! In breakdown, the ready-to-hand shows a presence-at-hand that had been in the background.

options.html: It is the stance of theoretical knowing
options.text: It is the stance of theoretical knowing
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Heidegger treats the theoretical stance as regarding things as present-at-hand.

options.html: It is the original way we encounter things
options.text: It is the original way we encounter things
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. For Heidegger, presence-at-hand is derivative. We first encounter things as ready-to-hand in use.

options.html: It is a false view that should be avoided
options.text: It is a false view that should be avoided
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger doesn't call presence-at-hand false. It's a legitimate stance, including the stance of science, but a derivative one.

forms.stemHtml: You reach for your reading glasses to check a detail, and they aren't where you left them. The more you need them, the more their absence stands out. Which mode of breakdown is this? Enter one word.

options.html: obtrusiveness
options.text: obtrusiveness
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! When equipment is missing, its absence obtrudes. Heidegger calls this obtrusiveness.

options.html: conspicuousness
options.text: conspicuousness
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Conspicuousness is when equipment is damaged or unusable. Missing equipment shows up as obtrusiveness.

options.html: obstinacy
options.text: obstinacy
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Obstinacy is when something stands in the way. Missing equipment shows up as obtrusiveness.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. When equipment is missing, the mode of breakdown is obtrusiveness.

forms.stemHtml: Heidegger calls theoretical knowing a "founded" or derivative mode. What does he mean?

options.html: That theory is unreliable and should be replaced by practice
options.text: That theory is unreliable and should be replaced by practice
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Heidegger doesn't reject theory. He holds that it arises from, and depends on, involved dealings with things.

options.html: That it arises when involved dealings with things are held back
options.text: That it arises when involved dealings with things are held back
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Theoretical knowing regards things as present-at-hand, which becomes possible when involved use is held back.

options.html: That it's founded on the measurements taken in the sciences
options.text: That it's founded on the measurements taken in the sciences
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. It's the other way around. The measuring stance itself is founded on involved being-in-the-world.

options.html: That it comes first and practical use is built on top of it
options.text: That it comes first and practical use is built on top of it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That reverses Heidegger's order. Involved use comes first. Theoretical knowing is derivative.

title: Ready-to-Hand and Present-at-Hand
